title: Control before ownership: the land acquisition toolkit
summary: A developer rarely needs to own land on day one; he needs to control it while he proves the deal. This lesson lays out the tools in order of commitment, from a confidentiality agreement to a landowner joint venture, and shows how to choose the tool that matches the risk you have not yet resolved.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the best land deals buy time before they buy land. Every tool in this lesson exists to give you control of a site while the diligence and approvals that decide its value are still open, at a price you can afford to lose.

Recall

Q. When is a planning approval final?

A. When the appeal period has expired with no appeal filed, or any appeal has been finally decided. A council vote alone is not final.

Q. What is residual land value?

A. Gross development value, minus total development cost excluding land, minus required developer profit. It is the most a rational developer can pay for the land.

Q. Why should you scope an adviser's engagement in writing?

A. Because an adviser answers the question they were asked. A written scope makes sure they look where the risk actually is, and records what they were and were not engaged to do.

Why this matters

Last week you learned that density not yet granted must not be paid for in advance. This week answers the obvious question: then how do you hold a site long enough to win it? The answer is a set of acquisition tools, each trading a smaller, certain cost now for the right to decide later. Pick the wrong tool and you either lose the site to a faster buyer or own a site you should have walked away from. Omar will add a second question throughout the week: whichever tool you use, which entity signs it, because the paper you sign today decides who owns the site, the risk and the tax result later.

The ladder of commitment

Plain English first. Think of acquisition as a ladder. Each rung commits you more and gives the seller more certainty.

  1. Confidentiality agreement. Often called a non-disclosure agreement. You promise to keep the seller's information private; the seller shares surveys, leases, reports. No commitment to buy.
  2. Letter of intent. A short document setting out the main terms of a proposed deal: price, deposit, conditions, timing. Usually most of it is expressly not binding, though some clauses, such as confidentiality and exclusivity, often are.
  3. Option to purchase. You pay the owner a fee, called the option premium, for the exclusive right, but not the obligation, to buy at an agreed price within a set period. If you do not exercise, you lose the premium and nothing more.
  4. Conditional agreement of purchase and sale. A binding contract to buy, subject to conditions such as satisfactory diligence, financing or approval. If a condition fails, you can usually terminate and recover your deposit, depending on the drafting.
  5. Unconditional purchase. All conditions waived or satisfied. You are committed.
  6. Landowner joint venture. Instead of selling, the owner contributes the land to the project in exchange for a share of the outcome. You need less cash up front; you take on a partner.

The professional framing: each tool allocates two things, the risk of the unknowns and the cost of waiting. The seller wants certainty and money; you want time and the right to leave. The art is matching the tool to the specific unknown that is still open.

Say that out loud now.

Which unknown is still open, and which tool lets me resolve it before I am committed?

Worked example one: option or conditional purchase?

Hypothetical round numbers. A site worth 2.25 million dollars at its as-of-right density. You want 12 months to test a rezoning before committing.

Path A, option. You pay a non-refundable premium of 60,000 dollars for a 12-month option at 2.25 million plus a step-up if the rezoning is approved. If the rezoning fails and you walk, you lose 60,000 dollars. If you exercise, the agreement may credit the premium against the price; whether it does is a negotiated term.

Path B, conditional purchase. You sign a binding agreement at the same price with a 225,000 dollar deposit, 10 percent, refundable if an approval condition fails within 12 months. Most sellers will not grant a 12-month approval condition, and if they do, the drafting of "fails" becomes the whole negotiation. Your deposit is at risk if you miss a notice date.

The option costs a certain 60,000 dollars but gives you a clean exit. The conditional purchase costs nothing if it works but ties 225,000 dollars to drafting risk. For a long, uncertain approval, the option usually fits better. For a short diligence period on a site you expect to buy, the conditional purchase usually fits better. These amounts and percentages are commercial practice, not standards.

Worked example two: the landowner who will not sell

The owner has held the land for decades, does not need the cash, and does not want a tax bill on a sale. Hypothetically, she contributes the land at an agreed value of 2.25 million dollars into a joint venture. You contribute 3 million dollars of cash equity and run the development. On a simple pro rata basis, she holds 2.25 divided by 5.25, about 43 percent, and you hold about 57 percent, before any promote for your development work. You saved 2.25 million of cash; you gained a partner whose land value, timing of contribution and rights in a dispute must all be written down. Day 5 works the numbers fully. Whether contributing land avoids or defers tax depends on the system and the structure; verify against the primary source.

Valuing contributed land

The single hardest number in a landowner joint venture is the land's agreed value. Too high and your cash buys too little of the project; too low and the landowner feels cheated when the value rises. Three disciplines help. Agree the value on the as-of-right basis, exactly as last week taught. Fix the date the value applies. And write down in advance what happens if an approval raises the land's value: does the uplift belong to the joint venture, to the landowner, or is it shared? That last question is the one most handshake deals never ask, and Day 2 shows why it matters.

The biggest risk

Signing a letter of intent you believe is non-binding and discovering that its exclusivity, cost or confidentiality clauses bind you, or that its terms are complete enough to be treated as a contract. The control: every letter of intent says in plain words which clauses bind and which do not, and your lawyer reviews it before you sign. Professional sign-off required: a real estate lawyer.

The beginner's mistake

Paying for speed with commitment. A beginner who fears losing a site offers an unconditional purchase. A professional offers the seller something else he values, such as a larger option premium, a faster closing once conditions are met, or a share of the upside, while keeping the right to walk.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: an option, a sale and a land contribution can each be taxed differently for buyer and seller; verify against the primary source. Liability: taking title brings environmental and occupier liability; an option does not. Banking: lenders will not lend against an option, so the option period must be funded from equity. Governance: a landowner partner needs defined decision rights from day one. Estate: an option or joint venture interest must be valued and transferable on death; check the drafting. Exit: a partner's consent may be needed to sell or refinance, so negotiate it now.

Callback

In Week 20, LEX taught that a letter of intent can bind in some clauses and not in others, and that the label on the document does not decide it. This week you use that knowledge every time you put an offer in writing.

Recap

Climb the acquisition ladder only as far as the open unknowns require. Use options for long, uncertain approvals, conditional purchases for short diligence, and a landowner joint venture when the owner will not sell, with the land's value, its date and its uplift written down. Next: Ford, with Cole, on a handshake partnership that broke when the land rose in value.
checklist: Name the specific unknown still open before choosing a tool
Mark every letter of intent clause as binding or not binding
Use an option when the approval period is long and uncertain
Use a conditional purchase when diligence is short and the site is expected
Confirm whether an option premium is credited against the price
Fix a landowner's contributed value on the as-of-right basis, with a date
Write down who owns any approval uplift on contributed land
Have a real estate lawyer review every document before signing
head: Field checklist
speak: A developer rarely needs to own land on day one. He needs to control it while he proves the deal. The tools form a ladder. A confidentiality agreement gets you information. A letter of intent sets the main terms, usually mostly non-binding, but some clauses often bind. An option gives you the exclusive right to buy at an agreed price for a set time, for a premium you can afford to lose. A conditional purchase is a binding contract with exits if conditions fail. An unconditional purchase commits you. A landowner joint venture lets an owner who will not sell contribute land for a share. Match the tool to the unknown still open: options for long approvals, conditional purchases for short diligence. For contributed land, fix the value on the as-of-right basis, fix its date, and write down who owns any approval uplift.
terms: Option to purchase — a paid right, without obligation, to buy property at an agreed price within a set period.
Conditional agreement of purchase and sale — a binding contract to buy that either party may end if a stated condition is not satisfied or waived in time.
Contributed land — land an owner puts into a joint venture at an agreed value in exchange for an equity interest instead of cash.

hostile.q: You want a 12-month option for 60,000 dollars. Why should I take my land off the market for a year for that?
hostile.a: Because you keep the 60,000 dollars whatever happens, you keep the land if I walk, and if the rezoning succeeds you are paid the as-of-right price plus a share of the uplift you could not capture on your own. If the premium is too low for the time, tell me what term or amount would work, and I will price it against the approval risk.

role: Failure forensics (with Cole, audit and integrity)
title: The handshake that broke when the land went up: a composite
summary: A landowner and a developer agreed to build together on a handshake. When an approval doubled the land's value, they discovered they had never agreed what the land was worth, when that value was fixed, or who owned the uplift. This composite case runs the seven steps and ends with the rule that prevents it.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a handshake records the trust two people feel on the day they shake. It records nothing about what happens when the land under them doubles in value, and that is exactly the day the handshake is tested.

Recall

Q. What does an option premium buy?

A. The exclusive right, but not the obligation, to buy at an agreed price within a set period. If you do not exercise, you lose the premium and nothing more.

Q. In desk diligence, why must every finding have a source?

A. So you can produce the evidence later to a lender, a partner, a buyer or a court. A finding without a source is an opinion.

Q. What does legal privilege protect, in concept?

A. Certain confidential communications with a lawyer made for legal advice, so they cannot usually be forced into evidence. Its scope varies by system and it can be lost by sharing the advice widely; verify against the primary source.

Why this matters

Many first developments start with a relationship: a relative with land, a family friend, a farmer at the edge of town. These partnerships can be excellent, because the landowner brings the scarcest input at no cash cost. They are also the commonest source of litigation in small development, because the money that matters appears only after the work is done. This is a composite example built from patterns that recur. Names and numbers are invented. Watch especially for the moment the incentives reverse, because you will meet that moment in your own deals, and you will recognise it only if you have seen it named first.

The case in seven steps

Step 1, timeline. Year 0: a landowner and a developer agree, over dinner, to develop the landowner's 2,000 square metre lot together. "Fifty-fifty, you bring the land, I do the work." The land is zoned for about 45 units. Months 1 to 10: the developer spends 250,000 dollars of his own money on design, studies and a rezoning application, invoices addressed to him personally. Month 14: council approves 70 units. Month 15: an appraisal puts the land at 3.5 million dollars, up from about 2.25 million. Month 16: the landowner's adult children ask what "fifty-fifty" means. Month 18: the landowner receives an offer from a national builder to buy the rezoned land outright. Month 20: lawyers.

Step 2, key decisions. Starting work without a written agreement. Paying project costs personally rather than through a project entity. Filing the rezoning in the landowner's name, as the registered owner, with no agreement recording the developer's interest in the result.

Step 3, assumptions. The developer assumed "fifty-fifty" meant half the profit after the land was credited at its old value. The landowner assumed it meant she kept her land at whatever it became worth and split the building profit. Both assumptions were reasonable. They were also incompatible, and neither had ever been said aloud.

Step 4, incentives. Before the approval, the landowner needed the developer's money and skill. After it, she held a valuable asset and had a cash buyer who needed neither. The developer's leverage disappeared the moment his work succeeded. Incentives that line up at the start can reverse at the moment of value creation.

Step 5, warning signs ignored. The landowner deferred signing "the paperwork" three times. The children were never part of the conversations. The developer's lawyer had sent a draft term sheet in month 3 that was never answered. Each delay was treated as politeness rather than as information.

Step 6, point of no return. Filing the rezoning in the landowner's sole name without a signed agreement. From then on, every dollar of value the developer created attached to an asset he had no recorded interest in.

Step 7, root cause. Three numbers were never agreed: the land's contributed value, the date that value was fixed, and the ownership of any uplift from approvals. Everything else in the dispute flowed from those three blanks. None of them would have taken more than an afternoon to agree in month one.

Say that out loud now.

Value, date and uplift. If those three are not written and signed, there is no partnership, only a hope.

Worked example one: the two meanings of fifty-fifty

Hypothetical round numbers. The completed 70-unit project is worth 28 million dollars, at 400,000 dollars a unit. Development cost excluding land is 20.3 million.

The developer's reading: land credited at its old value of 2.25 million. Profit is 28 million minus 20.3 million minus 2.25 million, which is 5.45 million, split equally, 2.725 million each, after the landowner is repaid her 2.25 million. The landowner receives about 4.98 million in total.

The landowner's reading: land credited at its new value of 3.5 million. Profit is 28 million minus 20.3 million minus 3.5 million, which is 4.2 million, split equally, 2.1 million each, after she is repaid 3.5 million. She receives 5.6 million in total. The difference between the two readings is about 625,000 dollars, created by one undefined word.

Worked example two: what the developer could recover

With no written agreement, the developer's strongest claim may be for the value of his work and his 250,000 dollars of costs, through whatever restitution or implied-agreement remedies the local law allows, which is uncertain and slow. Against a share of a 5.45 million dollar profit, recovering 250,000 dollars plus some fees after two years of litigation is a near-total loss of the upside he created. The legal remedies are concepts only; verify against the primary source. Professional sign-off required: a litigation lawyer, before you assume any remedy exists.

Cole's audit note

Cole would ask for four documents and find none. A signed term sheet with the contributed land value and its valuation date. An agreement stating who owns approval uplift. Evidence that project costs were paid by a project entity both parties owned. And a record of what was promised to whom. Cole would add that the children's question in month 16 was the most valuable warning in the file: when people who were absent from the handshake start asking what it meant, the handshake has already failed.

Reading it from the landowner's side

The landowner is not a villain. She trusted a man who said he would do the work, and she reasonably believed that land she had owned for thirty years remained hers. When a buyer offered her cash, she did what most owners would do and asked what she was obliged to do. Nobody could tell her. A written agreement would have protected her as much as him: it would have told her what she had promised, and it would have given her children a document to read instead of a story to doubt.

The biggest risk

Spending money that creates value on an asset you do not own and have no recorded interest in. The control: no dollar goes into design, studies or approvals on a landowner's site until a signed agreement or an option records your interest and the three numbers.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that writing things down signals distrust. It does the opposite. A written agreement protects the relationship by removing the questions that would otherwise end it.

Callback

In Week 3, Kema taught that incentives drive behaviour and that loss aversion makes people fight harder to keep a gain than to win it. This case is both lessons at once: the approval moved the incentives, and the landowner was now defending a gain she felt was already hers.

Recap

A handshake partnership spent money on an asset one party owned, with no written value, valuation date or uplift ownership. When an approval raised the land's value, the two readings of "fifty-fifty" diverged by hundreds of thousands of dollars and the developer's leverage vanished. Rule 33 below is the control. Next: Roman on The Money, what control costs and what it buys.
checklist: Sign a term sheet or option before spending on a landowner's site
Write the contributed land value and its valuation date
State who owns any uplift from approvals
Pay project costs through an entity both parties own
Bring the landowner's family or advisers into the conversation early
Treat repeated delays in signing as information, not politeness
Have each party take independent legal advice
head: Field checklist
rule: Rule 33: No landowner partnership runs on a handshake; the land's agreed value, the date it is fixed, and who owns any uplift are written and signed before I spend a dollar on the site.
speak: This is a composite case. A landowner and a developer agreed over dinner to go fifty-fifty: she brings the land, he does the work. He spent 250,000 dollars of his own money and won a rezoning filed in her name. The land's value rose from about 2.25 million to 3.5 million, and then they found out that fifty-fifty meant two different things. Credited at the old value or the new one, the gap was about 625,000 dollars. Then a builder offered her cash, and his leverage disappeared. The point of no return was filing the rezoning in her sole name with no signed agreement. The root cause was three blanks: the land's agreed value, the date it was fixed, and who owns the uplift. Rule 33: no landowner partnership runs on a handshake; value, date and uplift are signed before I spend a dollar.
terms: Valuation date — the date at which an asset's agreed value is fixed for the purposes of an agreement.
Approval uplift — the increase in land value caused by an entitlement such as a rezoning.
Restitution — in concept, a legal remedy that returns the value of a benefit one party conferred on another without a contract to govern it.

hostile.q: You are asking an older landowner to sign a detailed agreement before you have shown her anything. Won't that frighten her off?
hostile.a: It may slow her down, and that is fine. I will explain each of the three numbers in plain words, encourage her to have her own lawyer and her family read it, and pay for her independent advice if that helps. A partner who will not write down what the land is worth before the work starts will not agree on it after the work succeeds.

title: What control costs and what it buys: options, carry and the price of walking away
summary: Owning land while you wait is expensive and hard to undo; controlling it with an option costs less and lets you leave. This lesson prices the two paths, shows how extensions and credits change the answer, explains why a lender will not fund an option, and ends with Warrick's view of option money on a personal balance sheet.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the cheapest way to own a bad site is never to have owned it. An option is the price you pay to keep that choice, and it is almost always smaller than the cost of buying first and discovering later.

Recall

Q. In the community hall, what do you show residents first, and why?

A. The as-of-right building the rules already allow. It turns the debate from "your project or nothing" into "this design or that one."

Q. Why is diligence spending best thought of as buying an option?

A. Because a modest certain cost buys the right to walk away before a much larger, irreversible commitment. Its value is the loss it lets you avoid.

Q. How should a large adviser fee be judged?

A. Against the decision it supports and the risk it reduces, with a defined scope and deliverable, not against the cheapest quote.

Why this matters

Land does not pay you while you wait. Interest, property tax and insurance run every month, and if the deal dies you must sell the land back into the market, often at a loss and with selling costs. When you are a small developer with finite equity, the difference between holding a site through an option and holding it through ownership can be the difference between surviving a failed approval and being stuck with land you cannot use or sell.

The cost of owning while you wait

Plain English first. If you buy the land now, you pay three kinds of cost while you prove the deal: the cost of the money tied up, the running costs of the land, and, if it fails, the loss on selling it again. The professional framing calls the first two carry and the third exit loss.

Worked example one, hypothetical round numbers. A site at 2.25 million dollars. You need 12 months to test a rezoning. You judge a 60 percent chance the deal proceeds.

Path A, buy now. Carry at a hypothetical 9 percent cost of money is 202,500 dollars; property tax and insurance add 20,000. Twelve-month carry: 222,500 dollars, paid whether the deal proceeds or not. If it fails, you resell at a discount and with costs, say a net 2.0 million, an exit loss of 250,000 dollars. Expected cost: 222,500 plus 0.4 times 250,000, which is 222,500 plus 100,000, or 322,500 dollars.

Path B, option. A 60,000 dollar premium for 12 months, credited against the price if you exercise. If the deal proceeds you lose nothing, because the premium becomes part of the price. If it fails you lose 60,000 dollars. Expected cost: 0.4 times 60,000, which is 24,000 dollars. You still carry the cost of your equity on the premium, which is small.

The option is cheaper by about 300,000 dollars of expected cost, and it caps your worst case at 60,000 dollars instead of 472,500. That cap is the real product. These figures and the premium level are commercial practice, not standards.

Say that out loud now.

An option caps my worst case. Owning while I wait does not.

Worked example two: extensions and the downside timeline

Approvals run late. Suppose the option is 12 months with two 6-month extensions available at 30,000 dollars each, not credited against the price. Your base case is approval at month 12. Your downside case, which you must fund, is month 24.

  • Base case: 60,000 dollars of premium, all credited on exercise. Net cost if you buy: zero.
  • Downside case: 60,000 credited plus 60,000 of extension fees not credited. Net cost if you buy: 60,000 dollars. If you walk at month 24: 120,000 dollars.
  • Compare owning for 24 months: about 445,000 dollars of carry before any exit loss.

Two lessons. First, negotiate the extensions at the start, when you have leverage, not at month 11, when the landowner knows you are stuck. Second, budget the downside, because an option that expires one month before the approval arrives returns nothing at all.

What the lender sees

A lender will not lend against an option, because an option is not an interest it can take as security in any useful way; there is no land to sell if you default. So the premium, the extensions and the pursuit costs come entirely from your equity. That shapes your capital plan: the option period is the most equity-intensive part of the project per dollar of value controlled, and it is unleveraged. A lender will also look at the option agreement itself when you come to finance the purchase, to confirm the price, the exercise date and that nothing registered on title ranks ahead of the purchase. Ask your lawyer whether the option should be registered or noted on title so a later buyer or lender of the seller cannot defeat it; verify the mechanism where you build.

When an option is the wrong tool

An option is not always cheaper. If the only open question is a short title and environmental review, a conditional purchase with a 60-day diligence period and a refundable deposit costs you nothing if it works and keeps the seller committed, which an option does not. An option also gives the seller a free look at the market: if the land rises sharply during the option period, a seller who regrets the price will read every clause looking for a reason your exercise notice failed. And a landowner who needs cash now may simply refuse a premium that only pays a fraction of the price. Choose the option when the unknown is long and expensive to resolve, such as an approval; choose the conditional purchase when it is short and cheap, such as desk diligence.

How the best do it

Many large homebuilders in North America describe their strategy as controlling land through options and similar contracts rather than owning it outright, so that a market downturn costs them option deposits rather than write-downs on owned land. The principle a small developer can copy is not the scale but the logic: pay a known amount for the right to decide later, and keep owned land on the balance sheet only when it is about to be built on.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On a personal balance sheet, an option premium is a wasting asset: it is worth something today and zero on the expiry date if unused. It should be held in the risk-capital tier, with pursuit costs, never funded from the liquidity floor you keep for life and emergencies. Warrick would also warn about concentration: three options on three sites in one town, all waiting on the same council, are one bet, not three. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal allocation.

The biggest risk

Letting the option lapse by missing a notice. Options are usually read strictly: an exercise notice sent late, to the wrong address or in the wrong form may be ineffective, and the premium is gone. The control is a deal calendar with every option date, extension date and notice requirement, owned by one named person and checked weekly.

The beginner's mistake

Comparing the option premium with zero. The beginner sees 60,000 dollars and thinks it is expensive. The professional compares it with the 322,500 dollars of expected cost of owning while waiting.

Callback

In Week 7, Warrick taught the liquidity floor: the cash you keep so that no single deal can force a personal crisis. Option money and pursuit costs are exactly the spending that must sit above that floor, because both can go to zero on a single council decision.

Recap

Owning while you wait costs carry and, if the deal fails, an exit loss. An option costs a premium and caps the worst case. Negotiate extensions early, budget the downside timeline, fund the option period from equity because no lender will, and hold option money in the risk-capital tier of your own balance sheet. Next: LEX on The Rules, what makes letters of intent, options and conditions binding, with a Canada and Guyana comparison.
checklist: Compare the expected cost of owning while waiting against the option
Cap your worst case before choosing a path
Negotiate extension rights and fees at the start
Fund the option period for the downside approval timeline
Ask whether the option should be registered or noted on title
Put every option and notice date on a calendar owned by one person
Hold option money in the risk-capital tier, above your liquidity floor
head: Field checklist
speak: Owning land while you prove a deal costs you carry every month and, if the deal fails, a loss when you sell it again. On a 2.25 million dollar site with a 60 percent chance of proceeding, buying now has an expected cost of about 322,500 dollars over a year. A 60,000 dollar option, credited against the price if you exercise, has an expected cost of about 24,000 dollars, and it caps your worst case at 60,000. That cap is the product. Negotiate extension rights at the start, while you have leverage, and budget the downside timeline. No lender will fund an option, so the option period comes from your equity. Ask whether the option should be noted on title. Put every notice date on a calendar owned by one person, because options are read strictly. On your own balance sheet, option money is risk capital.
terms: Exit loss — the loss realised when land bought for a project is resold after the project fails, including selling costs and any discount.
Option extension — a right in an option agreement to lengthen the option period, usually for an additional fee.
Wasting asset — an asset whose value declines to zero by a known date, such as an unexercised option.

hostile.q: Your option has no value as security. Why should I as your equity partner fund a premium we may lose?
hostile.a: Because it is the cheapest way to control the site while we test the rezoning. The worst case is losing 120,000 dollars of premium and extensions. Buying the land now carries about 445,000 dollars of carry over the same downside period plus an exit loss if it fails. The option is the smaller bet, and it is sized inside our risk-capital budget.

title: What binds before closing: letters of intent, confidentiality, options and conditions
summary: Before a land deal closes, its documents bind in ways that surprise people: a non-binding letter can bind, an option can be lost on a late notice, and a condition can belong to only one party. This lesson explains the concepts, how to draft for them, and how Canada and Guyana approach land contracts at a conceptual level.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a document binds because of what it says and how the parties behaved, not because of its title. Before closing, your job is to make sure every page binds exactly as much as you intend, and no more.

Recall

Q. What was the most serious challenge Cole raised in last week's Auditor's Chair memo?

A. That the full price was due on closing at a density not yet granted, breaking Rule 32, and that almost nothing in the file predated the price.

Q. What does "buyer beware" mean for land?

A. In concept, the seller usually has no general duty to disclose defects, so the buyer must find them through diligence and protect himself through conditions, warranties and indemnities. The limits of the principle vary; verify against the primary source.

Q. Who should engage the lawyer whose advice you want to be privileged?

A. You, or the entity you control, so the lawyer's client is the party seeking advice. Advice obtained through someone else may not carry the same protection; verify against the primary source.

Why this matters

Most land disputes are not about the closing documents. They are about the papers signed before them: a letter of intent one party thought was a contract, an option exercised a day late, a condition one party waived that the other thought was shared. You will sign these documents yourself, often under time pressure. The concepts below let you instruct your lawyer precisely and read a draft with your eyes open. Professional sign-off required: a real estate lawyer, on every document in this lesson.

Letters of intent and confidentiality agreements

Plain English first. A letter of intent is meant to record the main deal terms so both sides can decide whether to spend money on a full contract. The trouble is that common-law courts generally ask whether the parties intended to be bound and whether the essential terms are certain enough. A letter that names the land, the price, the deposit and the closing date, and is signed, can come close to a contract if it does not say otherwise.

The professional framing: draft every letter of intent with an express statement that it is not binding except for named clauses, and list those clauses. The usual binding ones are confidentiality, exclusivity for a period, each side paying its own costs, governing law, and the statement that no contract exists until a definitive agreement is signed. Some systems also impose duties of honesty or good faith in performing a contract; in Canada, the Supreme Court's 2014 decision in Bhasin v. Hrynew is widely taught for a duty of honest performance. How far such duties reach into negotiations is a question to verify against the primary source.

A confidentiality agreement should say what information is covered, what you may use it for, who you may share it with, such as lenders and advisers, and what happens when talks end. Sellers sometimes add a non-circumvention clause, a promise not to deal with their contacts directly, which can restrict you for years. Read it.

Worked example one, hypothetical. Your letter of intent says: "Price 2,250,000 dollars, deposit 10 percent, closing in 90 days, subject to a definitive agreement." The seller then refuses to sign the definitive agreement and sells to another buyer. Can you enforce? Probably not, because "subject to a definitive agreement" signals no intent to be bound. Now reverse it: you sign a letter with no such wording, the seller treats it as accepted, and you walk away after diligence. You may face a claim. One sentence of drafting decides which side of that line you stand on.

Options

An option is, in concept, a promise by the owner to hold an offer open, made binding because you pay for it. Three drafting points matter most. First, the exercise mechanics: how notice is given, to whom, at what address, by what method and by what time. Courts in many common-law systems read option exercise strictly, so a notice that does not match the clause may fail. Second, what happens after exercise: the option should attach a complete form of purchase agreement, or the price, deposit and closing date at least, so exercise creates a contract rather than a negotiation. Third, protection against third parties: whether the option can be registered or noted on title so a later buyer or lender of the owner takes subject to it.

Do not confuse an option with a right of first refusal. A right of first refusal only gives you the right to match an offer the owner chooses to accept from someone else. It does not let you buy when you want, and it does not fix a price.

Say that out loud now.

An option lets me buy when I choose at a fixed price. A right of first refusal only lets me match someone else.

Conditions

A condition in a purchase agreement makes the obligation to close depend on an event: satisfactory diligence, financing, an approval. Four questions decide how it works. Whose benefit is it for? A condition for the buyer's sole benefit can usually be waived by the buyer alone; a shared condition generally cannot. What is the standard: "satisfactory to the buyer in its sole discretion" or "acting reasonably"? What is the deadline, and is time stated to be of the essence, meaning a missed date can end the deal? And what notice is required to satisfy, waive or rely on the condition?

Worked example two, hypothetical. Your agreement has an approval condition "for the mutual benefit of the parties," expiring on day 180. On day 170 approval looks near and you want to waive the condition and close. Because the condition is mutual, the seller may refuse to let you waive it, and if the market has risen, he may prefer the deal to die on day 180. If the condition had been for your sole benefit, you could have waived it yourself. The difference between "mutual" and "sole benefit" can be worth the whole upside.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

This is a conceptual comparison only; verify against the primary source before you rely on any of it. Canada: land law is mainly provincial, so the rules on writing requirements for land contracts, on registration, and on how options and agreements can be protected on title differ between provinces. Many provinces use a land titles or registration system in which the register itself carries great weight, and most retain some form of the old rule that contracts for land must be evidenced in writing. Guyana: the legal system draws on Roman-Dutch tradition in parts of its land law alongside English common law, and both a deeds-based process, in which a transfer of land is passed through the deeds registry after advertisement and an opportunity to oppose, and a separate land registration system exist for different areas [unverified — confirm independently]. The practical lesson is the same in both: confirm with local counsel how an option or agreement is protected against a third party before you pay a premium.

The biggest risk

Losing an option or a condition on mechanics: wrong notice address, a date counted incorrectly, the wrong signatory. The control is a notice protocol written into the deal calendar: method, address, signatory, delivery evidence and a send date several days before the deadline.

The beginner's mistake

Signing the seller's form. The first draft is written for the party who drafted it. Always have your lawyer mark up the seller's form, or better, send yours first.

Callback

In Week 19 you learned that law comes from legislation, from courts and from custom, and that a contract with no named governing law is an invitation to a fight about which system applies. Every pre-closing document in this lesson should name its governing law, and the Two Systems comparison shows why that is not a formality.

Recap

Mark every letter of intent clause as binding or not. Read confidentiality and non-circumvention clauses. Draft options with strict, clear exercise mechanics, an attached purchase agreement and protection on title. Make conditions for your sole benefit where you can, with clear standards, dates and notices. Next: JAX on The Numbers, valuing contributed land and splitting a landowner joint venture step by step.
checklist: State in every letter of intent which clauses bind and which do not
Check confidentiality agreements for use limits and non-circumvention clauses
Draft option exercise mechanics precisely: method, address, signatory, time
Attach a complete purchase agreement to every option
Ask local counsel how to protect an option against third parties
Make conditions for your sole benefit wherever possible
Diary every condition and notice date with a send date days before
Name the governing law in every pre-closing document
head: Field checklist
speak: Before closing, documents bind because of what they say and how the parties behave, not because of their title. A letter of intent that names the land, price, deposit and closing date can come close to a contract unless it says otherwise, so state which clauses bind: usually confidentiality, exclusivity, costs and governing law. Read confidentiality agreements for non-circumvention clauses. An option is a paid promise to hold an offer open; draft the exercise mechanics precisely, attach the purchase agreement, and ask how to protect it on title. Do not confuse it with a right of first refusal, which only lets you match someone else. Conditions turn on whose benefit they are for, the standard, the deadline and the notice. A sole-benefit condition you can waive; a mutual one you may not. Canada and Guyana differ in how land contracts are recorded, so confirm locally.
terms: Letter of intent — a document recording proposed deal terms, usually non-binding except for named clauses.
Right of first refusal — a right to match an offer the owner is prepared to accept from a third party, without a fixed price.
Time is of the essence — a contract term making stated deadlines strict, so missing one can end the agreement.

hostile.q: Our letter of intent is non-binding, so why are you spending legal fees on it?
hostile.a: Because a letter can bind in ways neither of us intends. Exclusivity, confidentiality and costs should bind; price and closing should not until the full agreement is signed. A few hundred dollars of drafting now is cheaper than arguing later about whether we had a contract.

title: Splitting a landowner joint venture, line by line
summary: A worked landowner joint venture from agreed land value to final distributions: capital accounts, ownership percentages, a preferred return, a developer promote, and then the same deal rerun with an uplift-sharing clause. Every figure is a hypothetical round number with its units.
body:
Mr Shabazz, in a landowner joint venture the land's agreed value is the number that decides everyone's share, so every other figure in the split is downstream of it. Today we build the split step by step and then change that one number to see how much money moves.

Recall

Q. Which acquisition tool fits a long, uncertain approval period?

A. Usually an option: a known premium buys the right to buy later at an agreed price, and the worst case is losing the premium.

Q. In a residual land value, which two costs are most often forgotten?

A. Finance costs and sales costs. Leaving them out inflates what you think you can pay for land.

Q. When should you challenge an adviser's advice?

A. When it conflicts with the facts you hold, rests on assumptions you have not confirmed, or cannot be explained in plain language. Ask what they relied on and what would change their view.

Why this matters

A landowner joint venture can let you build with far less cash than buying the land. The price of that saving is a partner, and the partner's share is set by arithmetic you must be able to do and explain at the kitchen table. If you cannot show a landowner exactly how her land becomes money, she will not trust the deal, and she will be right not to.

Step 1: agree the land value and its date

All figures hypothetical. The landowner's lot is zoned for 45 units. Using the residual method, its as-of-right value is 2.25 million dollars. The parties agree that value, fixed at the date the joint venture agreement is signed. That date matters because the joint venture will apply for a rezoning, and any value the approval creates arises after it.

Step 2: open the capital accounts

A capital account records what each partner has put in. The landowner contributes land credited at 2.25 million dollars. You contribute 5.3 million dollars of cash for design, approvals and the equity share of construction.

  1. Total equity: 2.25 million plus 5.3 million equals 7.55 million dollars.
  2. Landowner share: 2.25 divided by 7.55 equals 29.8 percent.
  3. Your share: 5.3 divided by 7.55 equals 70.2 percent.

Step 3: the project

The rezoning succeeds at 70 units. Each sells for 400,000 dollars, so gross development value is 28 million dollars.

  1. Development cost excluding land: 20.3 million dollars, including finance and sales costs.
  2. Total cost including the land at its credited value: 20.3 plus 2.25 equals 22.55 million dollars.
  3. Construction loan: 15 million dollars. Equity: 22.55 minus 15 equals 7.55 million, which matches Step 2.
  4. Profit: 28 million minus 22.55 million equals 5.45 million dollars.

After the loan is repaid from sales, 13 million dollars is available to the partners: their 7.55 million of capital plus the 5.45 million of profit.

Say that out loud now.

Capital back first, then the preferred return, then the promote, then the rest by share.

Step 4: the waterfall

A waterfall is the order in which cash is paid out. This one has four tiers, with terms that are commercial practice, not standards. Assume the project takes two years and the preferred return is 8 percent a year, simple, on capital.

  1. Return of capital. Landowner 2.25 million, you 5.3 million. Remaining: 13 minus 7.55 equals 5.45 million.
  2. Preferred return at 16 percent over two years. Landowner 0.16 times 2.25 million equals 360,000 dollars. You 0.16 times 5.3 million equals 848,000 dollars. Total 1.208 million. Remaining: 5.45 minus 1.208 equals 4.242 million.
  3. Developer promote of 20 percent of what remains, paid to you for running the project: 0.2 times 4.242 million equals about 848,000 dollars. Remaining: about 3.394 million.
  4. Balance by capital share. Landowner 29.8 percent of 3.394 million is about 1.011 million. You 70.2 percent is about 2.383 million.

Totals. Landowner: 2.25 plus 0.36 plus 1.011 equals about 3.62 million dollars. You: 5.3 plus 0.848 plus 0.848 plus 2.383 equals about 9.38 million dollars. Check: 3.62 plus 9.38 equals 13.0 million. The sum always has to return to the cash available; if it does not, a tier is wrong.

Equity multiples: the landowner turns land worth 2.25 million into about 3.62 million, about 1.61 times. You turn 5.3 million into about 9.38 million, about 1.77 times, higher because of the promote that pays for your work and risk.

Step 5: rerun with an uplift-sharing clause

The landowner's advisers ask for a share of the approval uplift. The approval raised the land's value by 1.25 million dollars, from 45 to 70 units at 50,000 dollars of land value per unit. You agree that half of that uplift, 625,000 dollars, is added to her capital account when the approval becomes final.

  1. Landowner capital: 2.25 plus 0.625 equals 2.875 million. Your capital: 5.3 million, unchanged. Total equity: 8.175 million.
  2. Shares: landowner 2.875 divided by 8.175 equals 35.2 percent; you 64.8 percent.
  3. Total cost with land at its new credit: 20.3 plus 2.875 equals 23.175 million. Profit: 28 minus 23.175 equals 4.825 million.
  4. Preferred return: landowner 0.16 times 2.875 million equals 460,000; you 848,000. Remaining: 4.825 minus 1.308 equals 3.517 million.
  5. Promote: 20 percent of 3.517 million is about 703,000. Remaining: about 2.814 million.
  6. Balance: landowner 35.2 percent is about 990,000; you about 1.824 million.

Totals: landowner 2.875 plus 0.46 plus 0.99 equals about 4.32 million; you 5.3 plus 0.848 plus 0.703 plus 1.824 equals about 8.68 million. Check: 13.0 million. The uplift clause moved about 700,000 dollars from you to the landowner. That is not a reason to refuse it; it is the price of a fairer deal, and now both of you can see it before signing, which is Rule 33 in numbers.

Step 6: the downside, using Step 4's terms

Show the landowner a bad outcome too. Suppose sales come in at 25 million dollars instead of 28. With costs unchanged at 22.55 million, profit is 2.45 million and cash available is 10 million.

  1. Capital back: 7.55 million. Remaining: 2.45 million.
  2. Preferred return: 1.208 million, as before. Remaining: 1.242 million.
  3. Promote at 20 percent: about 248,000 dollars, down from 848,000. Remaining: about 994,000.
  4. Balance: landowner about 296,000; you about 698,000.

Landowner total: about 2.91 million. You: about 7.09 million. Check: 10.0 million. Her total fell by about 710,000 dollars while yours fell by about 2.29 million, because the promote and your larger share absorb the shock first. That table, three rows of it, is often what wins a landowner's trust.

The biggest risk

Crediting the land at the value the seller hopes for rather than the as-of-right value, which quietly transfers the approval upside before the work is done. The control is to credit as-of-right value on the agreement date and handle any uplift by an explicit clause, with its trigger and amount written down.

The beginner's mistake

Forgetting the check. Every waterfall must sum back to the cash available. Most errors in a split are found by adding the totals and seeing they do not match. Professional sign-off required: an accountant on the capital accounts and a lawyer on the waterfall drafting; how each payment is taxed depends on the system, so verify against the primary source.

Callback

In Week 15 you learned that the equity multiple tells you how much money comes back and the internal rate of return tells you how fast. A landowner usually cares most about the multiple on her land; you care about both, because your cash had a cost every month. Show her the multiple and show yourself the rate.

Recap

Fix the land's value and its date, open capital accounts, run the project, then pay the waterfall: capital, preferred return, promote, balance by share, and check that the totals return to the cash available. An uplift-sharing clause is fair and has a price you can calculate. Next: JAX in The Room, the landowner's kitchen table.
checklist: Fix the contributed land value on the as-of-right basis, with a date
Open capital accounts for land and cash contributions
Compute ownership percentages from the capital accounts
Run the project to the cash available after the loan
Pay the waterfall tier by tier: capital, preferred return, promote, balance
Check that the distributions sum back to the cash available
Model any uplift-sharing clause before agreeing it
Have an accountant and a lawyer review the split
head: Field checklist
speak: In a landowner joint venture, the land's agreed value decides everyone's share. Fix it on the as-of-right basis, say 2.25 million dollars, at the signing date. Open capital accounts: her land at 2.25 million, your cash at 5.3 million, so she holds about 30 percent and you about 70. The project sells for 28 million against 22.55 million of cost, a profit of 5.45 million, leaving 13 million for the partners. Pay capital back first, then an 8 percent simple preferred return for two years, then a 20 percent promote to you for running it, then the rest by share. She ends with about 3.62 million, you with about 9.38, and the totals must add back to 13 million. If she negotiates half the approval uplift added to her capital, about 700,000 dollars moves to her. That is fair, and now you both see it before signing.
terms: Capital account — a record of what each partner has contributed to a venture, plus or minus its share of results and distributions.
Waterfall — the order and rules by which a venture's cash is distributed among partners.
Promote — a share of profit paid to the managing partner above its capital share, as reward for its work and risk.

hostile.q: Why should the landowner accept a 20 percent promote for you on top of your larger capital share?
hostile.a: Because I carry the work, the guarantees to the lender and the risk of failure, and the promote is paid only after she has her land value back and her preferred return. If the project underperforms, the promote shrinks first. I will show her the waterfall at three outcomes so she can see that she is paid before I am rewarded.

title: The landowner's kitchen table
summary: The most important land negotiations happen at a kitchen table, not a boardroom. This lesson scripts a meeting with a landowner and her son about an option or a joint venture: the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to be silent, and how to keep your state when the talk turns to family and money.
body:
Mr Shabazz, at a landowner's kitchen table you are not selling a deal; you are asking a family to trust you with something they may have held for generations. Win the trust first and the terms become much easier to agree.

Recall

Q. In the composite handshake case, what three numbers were never agreed?

A. The land's contributed value, the date that value was fixed, and who owned any uplift from approvals.

Q. When a broker sets a deadline to waive conditions, how do you treat it?

A. As a negotiating move, not as information about the land. You waive only when every diligence stream is complete, in writing and priced.

Q. What should you ask an adviser before accepting a recommendation?

A. What they relied on, what they did not look at, and what would change their view. Then decide.

Why this matters

Many of the best sites are not on the market. They belong to people who have never sold land and do not plan to: a widow with a field at the edge of town, two brothers who inherited a lot, a farming family. They will not respond to an offer letter. They respond to a person they can understand and trust. Learning to sit at their table well is one of the highest-value skills a small developer can build, and it cannot be delegated to a broker.

The scene

A kitchen in the afternoon. Mrs Ramdial, hypothetical, in her seventies, owns a 2,000 square metre lot her late husband bought. Her son Dev, an accountant, sits beside her. Tea is on the table. You are alone; you have one printed page with a simple sketch and three numbers, and no laptop open.

Lines to say

  • "Thank you for having me in your home. Before I say anything about a project, I would like to hear what this land means to your family."
  • "Mrs Ramdial, there are three ways we could work together. You could sell. You could give me an option, which means I pay you now for the right to buy later at an agreed price. Or you could keep an interest and be my partner. Each one suits a different family. Which matters most to you: cash now, keeping a share, or simply not being rushed?"
  • "The land today is allowed about 45 homes. On that basis it is worth about 2.25 million dollars. If we win permission for more, I would like you to share in that, and I will show you exactly how."
  • "Please take this to your own lawyer. I will pay for that advice if it helps."
  • "There is no deadline from me. Take the time you need."

Lines never to say

  • "Fifty-fifty, you bring the land, I do the work." Day 2 showed you why.
  • "I have another site lined up if this does not work." It is pressure, and an elderly owner will rightly hear it as a threat.
  • "You don't need to worry about the details." To a family protecting its largest asset, that is the most alarming sentence possible.
  • "The land is not worth much as it is." Even if true, it insults the memory attached to it. Say what it is worth and why, with the number.

Say that out loud now.

"Which matters most to you: cash now, keeping a share, or simply not being rushed?"

The question behind the question

When Mrs Ramdial asks, "What happens if you can't finish?", the real question is, "Will I lose the land my husband left me?" Answer that one: "Under an option, the land stays yours until you are paid in full. Under a partnership, your land is credited first and the agreement will say what happens if the project stops." When Dev asks, "How do we know your numbers are right?", the real question is, "Are you going to take advantage of my mother?" Answer by offering transparency: "Here is how I calculated it. Please check it, and ask your own appraiser if you wish."

Worked example one: answering the son's numbers

Dev pushes back: "A builder offered our neighbour 3 million." You do not argue the neighbour's deal. You show the method. "If a site is approved for 70 homes, each home supports about 50,000 dollars of land value, so the land could be worth 3.5 million once approved. Today it is approved for 45, which is 2.25 million. The gap is the approval, which nobody has yet. I am offering 2.25 million now, plus half of whatever extra value the approval creates, paid when it is final." Dev can check every number, and the gap now has a name.

Worked example two: when to stay silent

After you explain the three options, Mrs Ramdial looks at her son and says nothing. Do not fill the silence. Do not add a sweetener. Silence in a family decision is usually the family thinking, and anything you say interrupts it. Count slowly to ten in your head, drink your tea, and wait. If the silence runs long, say only, "Would it help if I left this page with you and came back next week?" Then leave.

Holding your state

Family land conversations can turn emotional: grief for a husband, a sibling dispute, a fear of being cheated. Do not take it personally and do not hurry to fix it. Lower your voice, slow your speech, and let the emotion run. Before you arrive, sit in your car with the engine off and take a few slow breaths with a long exhale; that is a practitioner habit, and check any breathing practice with your doctor. Decide beforehand the one thing you will not agree to on the day, such as any signature, so pressure has nowhere to land.

Cultural intelligence thread

Landowners in Canada and in Guyana come from many backgrounds, and no country has one way of doing business. Still, some general tendencies are worth knowing, as tendencies, not rules. In many Guyanese families, and in many immigrant families in Canada, land is held as a family legacy, decisions involve elders and adult children, and a relationship is expected before business is discussed. Directly pressing for an answer at the first meeting can read as disrespect. In many Canadian commercial settings, by contrast, people expect a clear written offer early and may read long relationship-building as evasion.

The practical skill is to read the person, not the stereotype. Ask who else should be part of the decision. Watch whether they want the numbers first or the story first. Follow their pace. And in every setting, put the agreement in writing in plain language, because trust that is not recorded fades when people who were not at the table start asking questions.

The biggest risk

Signing something at the first meeting because the mood is warm. Warmth fades; paper stays. The control: never sign at the kitchen table. Leave a summary, encourage independent advice, and sign at a later meeting with both lawyers' comments in hand.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the son as an obstacle. Family members who were not in the first conversation are exactly the people who broke the handshake in Day 2. Bring them in early, answer their questions fully, and the deal you sign will survive them.

Callback

In Week 5, Kema taught the bottom line first and the rule of three. At a kitchen table you reverse the first and keep the second: relationship first, then three clear choices, sell, option or partner, each in one sentence. Three is what a family can hold in mind without feeling sold to.

Recap

Listen to what the land means before talking about a project. Offer three paths and ask which matters most. Show every number and its method, name the approval gap, invite independent advice and never sign at the table. Read the family, not the stereotype. Next: Kema closes the week with six questions, a Red Pen drill on an option letter and a boardroom drill.
checklist: Ask what the land means to the family before discussing any project
Offer three paths in plain words: sell, option or partner
Show the as-of-right value and name the approval gap
Explain the method behind every number and invite checking
Invite independent legal and valuation advice, and offer to pay for it
Bring in every family member who will influence the decision
Never sign anything at the first meeting
Follow up with a plain-language written summary
head: Field checklist
speak: At a landowner's kitchen table you are asking a family to trust you with something they may have held for generations. Start by asking what the land means to them. Then offer three paths in plain words: sell, give an option, or keep an interest as a partner, and ask which matters most: cash now, keeping a share, or not being rushed. Name the as-of-right value and the approval gap, and offer a share of the uplift paid when the approval is final. Show your method so the family can check it, and offer to pay for their own lawyer. Never say fifty-fifty, never mention your other sites, and never tell them not to worry about the details. When the family goes quiet, stay quiet. Read the people in front of you, not a stereotype, and never sign at the first meeting.
terms: Independent legal advice — advice a party receives from its own lawyer, separate from the other side's, often recommended where one party is vulnerable.
Question behind the question — the underlying concern a person is expressing through a surface question.
Legacy land — land a family holds for its emotional and inherited meaning as much as its market value.

hostile.q: Dev says: you are a developer, so your job is to pay my mother as little as possible. Why should we believe anything you show us?
hostile.a: You should check it rather than believe it. Here is the method, the inputs and the as-of-right value. Have your own appraiser and lawyer review it, and I will pay for their time. If they find an error, I will correct it. I would rather pay a fair price to a partner who trusts me than win a low price from one who does not.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Land acquisition week review: six questions, a Red Pen option and the boardroom
summary: Six questions on the acquisition ladder, the cost of control, what binds before closing and how to split a landowner joint venture, then a recap of the week. The Red Pen drill plants defects in a hypothetical option letter, and the boardroom drill asks you to explain your acquisition approach in two minutes.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week's discipline is to control land only as far as the open unknowns require, and to write down every number a partner could later dispute. Today you show you can do both from memory.

Recall

Q. What is the expected cost of owning a site while you wait, compared with an option, in this week's example?

A. About 322,500 dollars over a year for owning, against about 24,000 dollars for a 60,000 dollar option credited against the price, on a 60 percent chance of proceeding. The option also caps the worst case at its premium.

Q. What does a Phase II environmental site assessment add to a Phase I?

A. Sampling of soil, groundwater or other media to test for contamination that the Phase I records review flagged as possible.

Q. Why does an engagement letter say who the client is?

A. Because the adviser's duties, and often privilege, run to the client. If an entity is the client, its partners may not be.

Why this matters

Land acquisition rewards people who can think clearly while the other side is pushing: a seller who wants commitment, a landowner's family that wants reassurance, a partner who wants speed. Answering aloud from memory is the practice that holds up under that pressure. Answer each question before you read the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the rungs of the acquisition ladder from least to most committed.

Answer: Confidentiality agreement, letter of intent, option to purchase, conditional agreement of purchase and sale, unconditional purchase. A landowner joint venture sits beside the ladder as an alternative to buying.

Question 2. When does an option usually fit better than a conditional purchase?

Answer: When the open unknown is long and costly to resolve, such as an approval. A conditional purchase usually fits a short, cheap unknown such as desk diligence.

Question 3. What is the difference between an option and a right of first refusal?

Answer: An option lets you buy when you choose at a fixed price. A right of first refusal only lets you match an offer the owner is willing to accept from someone else.

Question 4. Why does it matter whether a condition is for your sole benefit or mutual?

Answer: You can usually waive a condition for your sole benefit by yourself. A mutual condition may need the other party's agreement, so a seller who regrets the price can let the deal die.

Question 5. In this week's joint venture, how much did a clause giving the landowner half of the approval uplift move between the partners?

Answer: About 700,000 dollars, from the developer to the landowner, with total distributions still summing to 13 million dollars.

Question 6. What was Rule 33?

Answer: No landowner partnership runs on a handshake; the land's agreed value, the date it is fixed, and who owns any uplift are written and signed before I spend a dollar on the site.

Say that out loud now.

Say Rule 33 without looking, then name the three numbers it protects.

Recap of the week

Day 1, JAX: the acquisition ladder and matching each tool to the open unknown. Day 2, Ford with Cole: a composite handshake partnership that broke when a rezoning raised the land's value. Day 3, Roman: the expected cost of owning versus controlling, extensions, and why no lender funds an option. Day 4, LEX: what binds before closing, strict option mechanics, sole-benefit conditions, and a Canada and Guyana comparison. Day 5, JAX: a landowner joint venture split from capital accounts to waterfall, with an uplift clause and a downside case. Day 6, JAX: the kitchen table, three choices, and reading the family rather than a stereotype.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical option letter and find the defects before reading on.

Option, Lot C, hypothetical. The owner grants the developer the option to buy the land for 2,250,000 dollars, plus a fair share of any increase in value, to be agreed. Option period: about one year. Premium: 60,000 dollars, refundable if the developer decides not to proceed. Exercise: the developer will let the owner know. Extensions: available if needed. On exercise the parties will negotiate a purchase agreement in good faith. This option is personal to the developer. Signed by the developer and by the owner's son on her behalf.

The defects, revealed:

  1. "A fair share of any increase, to be agreed." An agreement to agree is the uplift question left blank, Rule 33 broken. State the share, the trigger and the date.
  2. "About one year." An option period must have a precise expiry date and time.
  3. A refundable premium. If the premium comes back whenever you walk, the owner has received little for holding the land, which can weaken the option's enforceability and invites a dispute. The premium is normally non-refundable and credited on exercise.
  4. "Will let the owner know." No method, address, form or time for exercise. Options are read strictly; this invites a fight over whether exercise happened.
  5. "Extensions available if needed." No number, length or fee. Negotiate them now while you have leverage.
  6. "Negotiate a purchase agreement in good faith." Exercise should create a contract. Attach the purchase agreement or at least its deposit, closing date and conditions.
  7. "Personal to the developer." You cannot assign it to the project entity or a lender. Allow assignment to an affiliate.
  8. Signed by the son "on her behalf." Ask for the authority: a power of attorney, its scope, and whether it covers land. Without it, the owner may not be bound.
  9. No governing law, no registration and no independent advice for the owner. Each is a later argument waiting to happen.

Boardroom drill

Set a two-minute timer and explain how you acquire land to an imaginary investment committee. Then compare with the model.

Model answer: "We control land before we own it, and only as far as the open unknowns require. For short diligence we use a conditional purchase with conditions for our sole benefit. For long approvals we use an option with a non-refundable premium credited on exercise, a fixed expiry, pre-agreed extensions and an attached purchase agreement. The option period is equity-funded and sized inside our risk-capital budget, because a lender will not fund it. Where an owner will not sell, we offer a joint venture with the land credited at its as-of-right value on a fixed date, and any approval uplift shared by a written formula. We model the waterfall at three outcomes and show it to the owner, encourage their own advice, and never sign at the first meeting. Every notice date sits on one calendar with a named owner."

Score yourself

Score your attempt from 1 to 5 on accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question. Accuracy: were the tools, numbers and terms correct? Structure: bottom line first, then tools, then controls? Composure: did you pause rather than rush? The hard question: did you say what you do when an owner refuses to write down the land value, which is that you do not spend on the site? Reread only the lesson behind your lowest score.

The biggest risk

head: The six questions
speak: This week's discipline is to control land only as far as the open unknowns require. The ladder runs from a confidentiality agreement to a letter of intent, an option, a conditional purchase and an unconditional purchase, with a landowner joint venture beside it. Options fit long approvals; conditional purchases fit short diligence. Owning while you wait costs carry and, if it fails, an exit loss; an option caps the worst case. Draft options with a fixed expiry, strict exercise mechanics, a non-refundable premium credited on exercise, pre-agreed extensions and an attached purchase agreement. Make conditions for your sole benefit. In a landowner venture, credit the land at its as-of-right value on a fixed date and share any uplift by a written formula. Rule 33: no handshake partnerships.
terms: Agreement to agree — a term leaving a key point to be settled later, which is often unenforceable and invites dispute.
Power of attorney — a document authorising one person to act legally for another, within a stated scope.
Assignment — the transfer of contractual rights to another party, which the contract may permit, restrict or forbid.

hostile.q: The option letter was signed by the owner's son. You have a signature. Why does his authority matter?
hostile.a: Because only the owner, or someone with authority to bind her over this land, can grant the option. If his power of attorney does not cover land, or he has none, the owner may not be bound, and my premium has bought nothing. I will ask for the power of attorney, check its scope with my lawyer, and have the owner sign herself with independent advice if possible.
